text: Time to go one level deeper than "rows move from source to destination." How do they actually move? The answer is the buffer, and it's one of the most important performance concepts in this entire course.

Moving a million rows one at a time would be painfully slow, so the data flow engine doesn't do that. Instead it allocates a block of memory — a buffer — fills it with as many rows as will fit, and passes that entire buffer down the chain to the next component. Every transformation and destination in your data flow processes a buffer at a time, not a row at a time. This is exactly what you're watching when the Data Viewer, which we'll cover in Lesson 18, pauses "buffer by buffer" while you step through it.

Two properties decide how big those buffers actually are. DefaultBufferSize defaults to ten megabytes — 10,485,760 bytes exactly. DefaultMaxBufferRows caps it at ten thousand rows by default. But here's the part that matters for real packages: a buffer's capacity is bytes, not rows. So a narrower row — fewer columns, smaller data types — lets more rows fit in that same ten megabytes. That's the actual reason experienced SSIS developers are strict about dropping columns a data flow doesn't need as early as possible. And if the machine genuinely doesn't have enough memory for the buffers a package needs, SSIS spools them to disk instead — watch the "Buffers spooled" counter, because a rising number there is a real performance problem.
Now that you understand how rows physically move, let's configure the component you'll build into almost every package you write: the OLE DB source and destination.
